\[
T^{(t)}(k) = \operatorname{round}\!\left(\frac{255}{M} \sum_{j=0}^{k} h^{(t)}_j\right),
\quad
I_{\text{out}} = \sum_{t} w_t(x, y)\, T^{(t)}(I),
\qquad
8 \times 8\ \text{tiles}
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(h^{(t)}_k\): The number of pixels of tile t at level k
- \(M\): The number of pixels in one tile
- \(T^{(t)}\): The curve of tile t
- \(w_t(x, y)\): The bilinear weight of tile t at the pixel

h^(t) is the histogram of tile t and M the number of pixels in a tile. Each tile gets the histogram equalization curve of its own pixels, rounded to whole levels. Each pixel blends the curves of the four nearest tile centers with bilinear weights w_t, as Pizer and colleagues describe for interpolated AHE. This is CLAHE without a clip limit, and it uses the same code. A flat tile has one tall bin, so its curve jumps steeply at that level. That stretches small differences, such as noise, to large ones.
